title: Year 2 Web Development Track
intro: 10 short weeks. Each week: one goal, one thing to find out from real people, one tiny build, and 3 check questions. Our own Yewa College sites are the examples — you will learn how they were made.

SS.name: Scam Shield
SS.job: Helps people spot scam messages before they lose money.

HC.name: Harvest Calendar Naija
HC.job: Shows which crops to plant and harvest each month.

AP.name: Apprentice Pathway Explorer
AP.job: Helps young people explore trades like tailoring, welding and hair styling.

weeks.title: What is a website, really?
weeks.goal: Know that every website is just a text file the browser reads, and make your first page.
weeks.look: Open Scam Shield. Find the big title, a paragraph and a button. Those are three HTML tags.

research.q: Ask 3 people at home: have you ever got a message you thought was a scam? What did it say?
research.tip: Write their answers in a few words. Real stories make your website matter.

build.task: Make a page with a title and one paragraph about scams.
steps: Open the Code Lab or any code app on the phone

Under it type

Press Run and look at your page

check.q: What does the browser read to show a website?
Which tag makes the biggest heading?
Why did Scam Shield get built?
opts: To help people spot scam messages

weeks.say: A website is a text file. HTML tags tell the browser what each part is.

trainer.open: Every website you have ever seen — Google, WhatsApp Web, Scam Shield — is just a text file. Today you'll write one.

weeks.title: Headings, lists and links
weeks.goal: Put information in order with headings, lists and links.
weeks.look: Open Harvest Calendar Naija. Notice how months and crops are grouped. Grouping = structure.

research.q: Ask a farmer, market seller or grandparent: which 3 crops are planted around the start of the rainy season?
research.tip: Write the crop and the month.

build.task: Make a list of 3 crops with the months they are planted, and a link to Harvest Calendar.
steps: Make a list with <ul> and three <li> items
Run it and tap the link

check.q: Which tag holds one item in a list?

opts: So people can find information fast

weeks.say: Headings, lists and links put information in order so people find what they need fast.

trainer.open: Information is easier to use when it's in order. Today you'll organise like Harvest Calendar does — with headings, lists and links.
props: Research answers about crops and months
plan: Show Harvest Calendar: how are months and crops grouped? Grouping = structure.
Teach <h2>, <ul>/<li> and <a href>. Build one list together.
Kids list 3 crops + planting months from their research, plus one link.
Swap phones: can a partner find a crop fast? Check questions.

weeks.title: Pictures and sections
weeks.goal: Add a picture with alt text and group content in sections, like a trade card.
weeks.look: Open Apprentice Pathway Explorer. Each trade is a card: picture, name, short facts.

research.q: Talk to one artisan near you (tailor, mechanic, hairdresser, welder). How long did they learn the trade? What tool matters most?
research.tip: Their answer becomes your card's facts.

weeks.say: Sections group things that belong together. Alt text makes pictures useful for everyone.

trainer.open: Pictures make people stop and look. Today you'll build a trade card like Apprentice Pathway does — picture, name and facts.

weeks.title: CSS: colour and fonts
weeks.goal: Use CSS to change colours and text so the page feels trustworthy.
weeks.look: Look at Scam Shield's colours. Warning parts look different from safe parts. That is CSS.

research.q: Show 3 classmates two colours: red and green. Ask: which one feels like danger? Which feels safe?
research.tip: Count the answers. Designers use what people already feel.

build.task: Style your scam page: a calm background, a strong title colour, and a red warning line.
build.code:
Stop Scams

Never share your BVN or PIN.

check.q: HTML is the structure. CSS is…

opts: People already link red with danger

weeks.say: CSS is the style. We used red for warnings because people already feel red means danger.

trainer.open: HTML is the skeleton. CSS is the clothes. Today you dress your scam page so people trust it.
props: Colour cards or a colour picker site
plan: Show the same page with and without CSS. Which feels safer to use?
Teach selector { property: value; } with background, color, font-size.
Kids style their scam page: calm background, strong title, readable text.
Gallery walk: which page is easiest to read? Why? Check questions.
lookfor: Uses a selector, braces and semicolons correctly
Text is readable (good contrast)
Can explain WHY they chose a colour
fix: Missing ; or }
CSS stops working after a mistake — check each line ends with ; and the block closes with }.
Bright yellow text on white
Ask a partner to read it from arm's length. Contrast matters.

weeks.title: Boxes that fit any phone
weeks.goal: Lay out cards in rows that wrap nicely on a small phone screen.
weeks.look: Open Apprentice Pathway on a phone, then on a bigger screen. The cards move to fit. That is a flexible layout.

research.q: Ask 5 people: do you use the internet more on a phone or a computer?
research.tip: This is why we build phone-first.

build.task: Put 3 trade cards side by side that wrap on a phone.
steps: Turn the phone sideways and watch

Hair styling

weeks.say: Flexbox lets the cards move to fit any screen, because most of our users are on phones.

trainer.open: Most people visit our sites on phones. Today you'll make boxes that fit any screen — like Apprentice Pathway's cards.
props: A phone and a bigger screen to compare
plan: Open Apprentice Pathway on a phone, then a laptop. What moves?
Teach display:flex, flex-wrap:wrap and gap. Show the box model (padding, margin).
Kids put 3 cards side by side that wrap on small screens.
Turn phones sideways and back — do the cards still fit? Check questions.
lookfor: Uses flex-wrap so cards wrap
Adds gap/padding so it's not cramped
Tests on a real phone
fix: Cards squash into thin strips
Give each card a min-width (e.g. 200px) so it wraps instead.
Forgets the container
flex goes on the box AROUND the cards, not on each card.

weeks.title: JavaScript events: when something happens
weeks.goal: Make a button do something when it is tapped (purple = events).
weeks.look: On Scam Shield, tap the check button. Something happens. That is an event: when tapped → do this.

research.q: Ask someone who uses POS or bank apps: which button do you tap most? What happens after?
research.tip: Every app is 'when this happens → do that'.

build.task: Make a button that shows a safety tip when tapped.
steps: Inside: document.getElementById('out').textContent = 'Banks never ask for your PIN.';

opts: Something that happens, like a tap

check.q: In Scratch, 'when this sprite clicked' is like which JavaScript?

weeks.say: Events are purple: when the button is tapped, the code runs. Same idea as 'when this sprite clicked' in Scratch.

trainer.open: Now we make the page DO something. In Scratch it was 'when this sprite clicked'. In JavaScript it's an event.
props: Scam Shield's tip button as the example
plan: Recall Scratch 'when clicked'. Same idea, new words: addEventListener('click').
Live-code a button that shows a tip. Kids say each line in plain words.
Kids build their own tip button with a tip from their research.
Predict-then-run: what happens if we change 'click' to 'dblclick'? Check questions.
lookfor: Can point to the event and the action
Uses getElementById correctly
Explains it as 'when … then …'
fix: Nothing happens on click
Check the id in HTML matches the id in JavaScript exactly — capital letters count.
Script runs before the button exists
Put the <script> at the bottom of the page.

weeks.title: Variables: boxes that remember
weeks.goal: Store what the user types in a variable and use it (blue = variables).
weeks.look: Apprentice Pathway remembers which trade you picked. A variable holds that choice.

research.q: Ask 3 classmates: which trade would you like to learn, and why?
research.tip: Use their answers to test your page.

build.task: Ask for a name and a trade, then greet the person.
steps: Add two inputs with ids name and trade, and a button
Show: 'Hi ' + name + ', ' + trade + ' is a great choice!'

opts: A labelled box that remembers something
Makes a box called name and puts a value in it

weeks.say: A variable is a blue box that remembers what the user typed, so the page can use it.

trainer.open: Variables are boxes that remember things — like the score box in Scratch. Today the page will remember your name.
plan: Recall the Scratch score variable. In JavaScript: let name = …
Live-code: read an input, store it in a variable, show a greeting.
Kids ask for a name and a trade and show 'Hello Ada, tailoring is a great choice!'.
Change the value, run again — what changed? Check questions.
lookfor: Uses let/const with a clear name
Reads .value from the input
Can say what's IN the box at each step
fix: Shows [object HTMLInputElement]
You stored the box, not what's in it — add .value.
Variable named x or a
Name it for what it holds: tradeName, userName.

weeks.title: Conditionals: if this, then that
weeks.goal: Make the page decide: if a message has scam words, warn the user (red = conditionals).
weeks.look: Scam Shield decides 'risky' or 'looks safe'. That decision is an if.

research.q: Collect 3 real scam words or phrases people have seen (e.g. 'urgent', 'you have won', 'send your BVN').
research.tip: Ask family. Never call or reply to a scammer.

build.task: Build a mini scam checker: if the message includes 'urgent', show a red warning.
steps: Add a textarea id="msg" and a Check button
Test with a scam message and a normal message

check.q: Which logic colour is if / else?
What happens if the condition is false?

weeks.say: Conditionals are red: if the message has a scam word, we warn; else we say it looks safe.

trainer.open: Real apps make decisions. IF the message says 'urgent', THEN warn the user. You're building a mini Scam Shield today.
props: 3 real scam messages from Week 1 research (with personal details removed)
plan: Read a scam message. What word makes it suspicious? That's our IF.
Live-code if / else with .includes('urgent'). Use the red colour.
Kids add 2 more scam words with else if, and test with real messages.
Try to trick a partner's checker. Check questions.
lookfor: Writes if/else with correct brackets
Tests with a safe message AND a scam message
Lowercases the text before checking (smart!)
fix: 'URGENT' isn't caught
Use message.toLowerCase() before .includes so capital letters don't fool it.
Only tests the scam case
A checker must also say 'looks okay' — test both.

weeks.title: Loops: do it again and again
weeks.goal: Use a loop to show a whole list without typing each item (green = loops).
weeks.look: Harvest Calendar shows many crops. Nobody typed each card by hand — a loop builds them.

research.q: Find 5 crops grown near your home and the month they are harvested. Ask a farmer or check with a parent.
research.tip: Your list becomes the data for your loop.

build.task: Store crops in a list and use a loop to show them all.
steps: Inside, add each crop to the page
Add a 6th crop to the list and watch it appear by itself

check.q: Why use a loop instead of typing 5 lines?
opts: It repeats work for us and grows with the list

weeks.say: Loops are green: the code repeats for every crop in the list, so adding data adds cards automatically.

trainer.open: Imagine writing the same line 50 times. A loop does the repeating for you — like 'forever' and 'repeat' in Scratch.
props: Harvest Calendar crop list as the example
plan: Recall Scratch 'repeat 10'. Show writing 5 crop lines by hand, then with a loop.
Live-code an array + for…of loop that shows each crop.
Kids store 5+ crops from research in a list and loop to show them.
Add one crop to the list — did the page update by itself? Check questions.
lookfor: Uses an array with [ ] and commas
Loop shows every item
Can explain why adding an item 'just works'
fix: Only the last crop shows
You replaced instead of added — use += or appendChild inside the loop.
Endless loop freezes the phone
Use for…of over the list so it stops at the end.

weeks.title: Put it together and show it
weeks.goal: Remix one of our three sites into your own mini version that uses all 4 logic colours, then explain it like a pro.
weeks.look: Pick Scam Shield, Harvest Calendar or Apprentice Pathway. What is ONE thing you would add for your community?

research.q: Show your mini site to 2 people who are not in ByteBusters. What confused them? What did they like?
research.tip: Fix one thing they said. Judges love that.

build.task: Build a mini site: HTML structure, CSS style, and JavaScript with a variable, an if, a loop and an event.
steps: Choose your site to remix and write your one new idea
Add the button (purple), a variable (blue), an if (red) and a loop (green)
Ask your trainer to help you put it online
Practise: 'The problem is… Our site helps by… I built…'

check.q: Name the 4 logic colours in order: variables, conditionals, loops, events
A judge asks 'what did YOU build?' The best answer…
opts: Names the exact part you made and why

check.q: Why did we ask real people questions every week?
opts: So our sites solve real problems
Because it is required by law

weeks.say: My site solves a real problem. I used structure, style, and all four logic colours — and I tested it with real people.

trainer.open: Today you put it all together — structure, style and logic — and prove you can explain every part.
plan: Show the 5 signs: Purpose, How it works, Logic, My decisions, Change it.
Kids combine HTML + CSS + one JS feature (event + variable + if).
Pairs: 60-second explain-back, partner asks one judge question; swap.
lookfor: Can find all 4 logic colours in their code
Answers 'how would you change it?' with a real step
Mentions real users from their research
fix: Copied code they can't explain
Ask them to change one line and predict what happens — then rebuild that part slowly.
Freezes on questions
Practise answers out of order; judges jump around.
